findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside a coroutine stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but its body contains no `await` — it calls `requests.get`, which is synchronous. Inside an async request handler this blocks the entire event loop thread for the whole duration of the billing call (up to the 5 second timeout), stalling every other concurrent request in that worker. Since this runs during request handling to render remaining quota, a slow or hung billing.internal will degrade the whole service rather than just this endpoint.

Use the httpx async client already used by `fetch_plan` on line 5-7, e.g. take an `httpx.AsyncClient` parameter (or construct one) and `response = await client.get(...)`. If a sync client is unavoidable, wrap it in `asyncio.to_thread(...)` and await that.

findings.title: New async function with blocking I/O has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that uses the blocking `requests.get` call inside an `async def`. There is no test exercising this function, so nothing would catch a regression in its behavior (e.g. wrong URL formatting, missing timeout, or the fact that it blocks the event loop). Since the PR's stated purpose is to fetch plan limits during request handling, at minimum a test verifying the function's return value/behavior against a mocked HTTP call should be added.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is f-string-interpolated straight into `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. If the value originates from a request parameter (path segment, query string, or JSON body), a caller supplying something like `../../admin/api-keys` or `1?x=`/`1#` can reach paths on the internal billing host other than `/limits/<id>` — an internal service that is presumably not otherwise reachable from outside. `requests` also follows redirects by default, so a billing-side redirect on an attacker-shaped path would be followed silently.

Fix: validate the identifier against its expected shape (e.g. UUID or integer) before use, or at minimum pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')`. Passing it as a parameter rather than a path segment, and setting `allow_redirects=False`, both reduce the blast radius.

Note on scope: the attacker is whoever supplies `tenant_id` to this coroutine; I could not see the call site, so I could not confirm that value is request-controlled or already validated upstream. That uncertainty is reflected in the confidence, not in the severity — if it is request-controlled, this is unauthenticated reach into an internal host.

findings.title: Bare except swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` are also absorbed — a Ctrl-C or a shutdown signal arriving during `_client.send` is silently discarded, and any programming error inside the client (AttributeError, TypeError) disappears with it. The PR description says "catch and log, then continue", but no logging happens on line 5, so failures are completely invisible.

Narrow this to the failures you actually mean to tolerate (e.g. `except Exception:` or, better, the client's transport/timeout exception types) and emit a log record with `logger.exception(...)` before returning.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently drops metrics failures with no log

findings.title: No test covers push_metrics' new failure-swallowing behavior
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics to catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating. No test file is included in this diff to verify that (a) a raising _client.send no longer propagates, and (b) the caller still proceeds normally / handles the None return correctly. If this catch were removed or the logic reverted, no test would fail.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates the counter without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, then yields control at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18 before writing on line 19. Any other coroutine scheduled during that yield sees the stale value, so two callers each holding `current = 999` with `cost = 1` will both pass the check on line 16 and both return `True`, admitting work above `LIMIT`.

The write on line 19 is also an absolute assignment of `current + cost` rather than a read-modify-write of the live value, so it discards any increment that `consume` (line 10) applied while `try_consume` was suspended — the counter can silently go backwards and the limiter under-counts indefinitely.

Fix by taking the existing lock around the whole check-and-update, mirroring `consume`:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

and drop the bare `await` from inside the critical section (or, if a real await is needed there, do it before acquiring the lock).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume bypasses _lock: rate limit defeated by concurrent requests

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's concurrency safety
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters, awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a genuine yield point), then writes back — all without holding _lock, unlike consume which uses the lock. A test that merely calls try_consume sequentially and checks the boolean return would pass even though concurrent tenants racing on this function can both pass the check and jointly exceed LIMIT. Since this PR's stated purpose is 'so a noisy client cannot starve everyone else,' the core guarantee (limit enforcement under concurrency) is exactly what's unverified.

findings.body:
The docstring says "Return (name, email) for a user." but the function now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` — a dict with an extra `tier` key, not a tuple. A caller following the docstring (e.g. via `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`) will get a wrong result or crash, since unpacking a 3-key dict yields its keys, not the documented values. Update the docstring to describe the actual dict shape and keys.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old tuple return contract

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller
findings.body: `lookup_user` previously returned a 2-tuple `(name, email)`; it now returns a dict with three keys. The retrieved caller `reports/weekly.py:6` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a 3-key dict into two names raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` at runtime for every call — and even if the dict had exactly two keys it would bind the keys, not the values, silently producing `"name <email>"`. Either update all callers to `u = lookup_user(...); u["name"], u["email"]`, or return a `NamedTuple`/dataclass that preserves backwards-compatible iteration.

findings.title: Return-shape change untested; existing caller would break silently
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple, but reports/weekly.py:render_row does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which unpacks a dict into its keys (not the intended values) rather than raising a clear error, or may raise ValueError depending on key count — either way this is a contract break. findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound by `if _, err := ...` and therefore only exists inside that `if` block; after logging it goes out of scope. Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error` that is never assigned and return it, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` on every path except validation failure.

Effect: a settlement row that fails to insert (constraint violation, deadlock, connection loss) is logged and the caller is told the write succeeded. For an end-of-day batch this means silently missing settlement records with no non-zero exit signal.

If the intent really is "log and continue", that decision belongs to the caller iterating the batch — this function should return the error and let the loop decide. Minimal fix:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("settlement insert: %w", err)
}
return nil
```

If swallowing is deliberate, drop the `error` return (or return a typed sentinel) so callers cannot be misled by a signature that promises failure reporting it never does. Note also the inconsistency: `validate` failures at line 12-14 *are* propagated, so the function looks like it reports errors.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Failed settlement insert is swallowed; function always returns nil

findings.title: WriteSettlement's error-return behavior is untested
findings.body: WriteSettlement always returns nil (see the shadowed `err` variable on lines 18-19) regardless of whether the db.Exec insert on line 15 fails. There is no test in this diff exercising WriteSettlement's return value on a failed insert, so this always-succeeds behavior would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so the same list object is reused on every call that omits the argument. Failed recipients from earlier calls remain in the list, so the second call returns its own failures plus all prior ones, and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "the failures for this batch" will get wrong results, and the leak is also a slow memory growth in a long-running process.

Use `attempted=None` and initialise inside: `if attempted is None: attempted = []`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Mutable default `attempted=[]` leaks recipients across calls

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries' mutable default argument bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument (attempted=[]) which will persist and accumulate across calls, since Python evaluates default arguments once at function definition time. No test in this diff exercises this function at all, let alone calls it twice to catch state leaking between invocations. A test asserting that two separate calls to send_with_retries with failing dispatches don't share/accumulate the 'attempted' list across calls would catch this immediately.

findings.title: Function named `send_with_retries` performs no retries
findings.body: The function is named `send_with_retries`, which strongly implies it will attempt to resend to a recipient more than once on failure. Looking at the body, each recipient is dispatched exactly once (`if not _dispatch([recipient], {})`) and failures are merely appended to a list and returned — there is no re-attempt loop, backoff, or retry count anywhere. A caller reading only the name (a reasonable thing to do for a public helper) would assume failed sends are retried automatically and could under-provision their own retry handling, silently losing messages on failure.

findings.title: Rounding comparison silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5
findings.body:
In a change advertised as a rename, `compute_rounding` also altered its comparison operator: the old body was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`, the new body is `return 1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. For the exactly-half case (`remainder_cents == 0.5`) the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1, i.e. round-half-up became round-half-down for that boundary. A remainder of exactly 0.5 is a routine input for a rounding helper, not a pathological one, so this will shift money by one cent on a real fraction of lines and the difference will not show up in any rename-focused review.

If the operator change is unintentional, restore `>=`. If it is intentional, it belongs in its own commit with a test pinning the `remainder_cents == 0.5` case and a note about the accounting impact; it should not ride along inside a rename.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > with no test coverage

findings.title: Off-by-one slice in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
`start` advances by `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11), but the slice ends at `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` (line 12), so each page yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items and the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page. For PAGE_SIZE=50 and 200 records, pages 0..3 return 49 items each and indices 49, 99, 149, 199 are silently omitted from the export — a data-loss bug that callers paginating until an empty page will not notice.

The existing `page_of` on line 6 uses `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, which is the correct form; `page_of_sorted` should match it:

    return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]

If the intent really were a short page, `start` would have to advance by `PAGE_SIZE - 1` too, but that would duplicate rows rather than skip them — the sibling function makes clear which behaviour is intended.

findings.title: New paginated+sorted export function has no test coverage
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices with `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, which drops the last record of every page (should be `start + PAGE_SIZE`). No test exists in this diff to exercise this function, so this off-by-one would ship silently — nothing would fail.

findings.title: Dropped nil guard raises AttributeError when purchase_order is None
findings.body:
`models/invoice.py` declares `purchase_order: "str | None"` and its docstring says the field is only set for customers on invoicing terms ("roughly one account in twenty"). The type therefore does *not* cover the nil case — removing the `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` check means `None.upper()` is evaluated for the ~95% of invoices without a PO, raising `AttributeError` on the normal rendering path.

There is a second, quieter contract change: `header_lines` previously returned a 1- or 2-element list depending on whether a PO existed; it now unconditionally returns 2 elements. Any caller that renders or counts these lines will now always emit a PO row.

Restore the conditional append (or build the list and conditionally extend it) before merging.

findings.title: Removed None-guard for purchase_order has no test covering the None case
findings.body: The diff deletes the `if invoice.purchase_order is not None` check and unconditionally calls `.upper()` on it. Per models/invoice.py, `purchase_order` is optional and unset for ~95% of invoices, meaning this will raise AttributeError for most invoices. No test in this PR exercises `header_lines` with `purchase_order=None`, so this regression would not be caught by the existing test suite.

findings.title: File handle leaks on early return and on exception paths
findings.body: `fh = open(path)` is not wrapped in a `with` block, and `fh.close()` on line 16 is only reached on the success path. When the header does not match, line 14 returns while the file is still open. Likewise, if `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) raises (empty file, decode error, malformed CSV), the handle is never closed. On CPython refcounting hides this most of the time, but under PyPy or when an exception traceback holds a frame reference the descriptor stays open — and an importer processing many partner catalogues can exhaust the fd limit. Use `with open(path) as fh:` around the whole body, matching the existing `read_rows` on lines 5-6.

findings.title: New read_validated function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_validated introduces new branching behavior (header mismatch returns None without closing fh, otherwise returns rows) but no test in this diff exercises it. A regression—e.g. the resource leak on the mismatched-header path (line 13-14 returns before fh.close() on line 16), or a change in the mismatch-detection logic—would go undetected.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(); can double-charge customers
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure *after* the gateway has accepted the POST (timeout, connection reset on the response, 5xx emitted after commit) causes a second and third `/charges` POST, each creating an additional charge. The customer is billed up to 3x.

The gateway docstring names the fix: it "supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." Generate a key once per logical charge (outside the retried function, e.g. in the caller or as a parameter of `charge_card`) and pass it through to `charge()`, so all retry attempts share the same key. Do not generate it inside the retried body — that would produce a new key per attempt and defeat the protection. If threading the key through is not feasible now, this function should not be retried at all.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7: `get_charge` is explicitly "Safe to repeat", so the retry there is fine. The new function does not share that property.

findings.title: No test guards against duplicate charges from retrying charge()
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge with @retry(attempts=3), but charge() is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge — unless an Idempotency-Key is passed, which this wrapper does not do. There is no test in this diff exercising charge_card under a simulated transient failure to verify it doesn't produce multiple charges (e.g. asserting the underlying POST/charge is invoked with an idempotency key, or that a failure-then-success sequence results in exactly one charge). As written, a regression that silently retries and double-charges a card would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: charge_card lacks a docstring noting the non-idempotency risk it inherits
findings.body: billing/gateway.py documents charge() as 'NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge' and says an Idempotency-Key header is needed to make retries safe. The new charge_card wraps charge() with @retry(attempts=3) but carries no docstring, and no Idempotency-Key is passed through. A caller reading only the name and signature (mirroring the safe fetch_charge/get_charge pair right above it) could reasonably assume retrying is safe here too, which contradicts the documented contract of the wrapped call. A short docstring calling out the risk (or documenting that an idempotency key must be supplied upstream) would prevent that misreading.

findings.title: expires_within subtracts naive datetime from tz-aware expires_at
findings.body: `datetime.now()` on line 9 returns a naive datetime (no tzinfo), while `invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails on every invocation regardless of input. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as the sibling function `is_expired` does on line 5. (The `.replace(microsecond=0)` is also a no-op for this comparison and can be dropped.)

findings.title: expires_within has no test, and would fail at runtime if exercised
findings.body: expires_within is new, untested code that subtracts a naive datetime.now() from invite.expires_at, which per models/invite.py is always tz-aware. Any call to this function would raise TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes. Nothing in the diff or repo exercises this function, so this defect would ship silently.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so for any account that has not completed onboarding this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. The PR description says the account payload is always present, but that is about `account`, not about `billingContact` — the sibling function on line 4 still guards the same field with `?.` and a default.

Mirror the existing pattern, e.g. return `account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""`, or change the return type to `string | undefined` and let callers decide. If a non-optional result is genuinely required, the input type should be narrowed to an account known to have a billing contact rather than assuming it.

findings.title: contactEmail has no test covering its behavior
findings.body: contactEmail is a new function that directly accesses account.billingContact.email without optional chaining, unlike bannerFor which uses `?.`. The Account type still marks billingContact as optional (`billingContact?: {...}`), so if this assumption ('always present on this page') is ever violated, this throws at runtime. No test exists for contactEmail, so neither the happy path (lowercasing) nor the crash-on-missing-billingContact scenario would be caught by the test suite.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch(url, timeout, retries=3)` documents `timeout` as being in MILLISECONDS and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `timeout=30` therefore gives the partner API 30 ms to respond, not the generous window the PR description intends. Worse, the docstring notes retries share the same budget, so all 3 default retries fall inside that 30 ms and the call will fail fast every night. Pass `timeout=30_000` (or whatever second-count is intended, multiplied by 1000).

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering its behavior
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue calls fetch(url, timeout=30) with no accompanying test. fetch()'s timeout parameter is documented as milliseconds, so timeout=30 means 30ms — the opposite of the 'generous' timeout described in the PR. A test asserting the value passed to fetch (or that the call succeeds within the intended window) would have caught this immediately; right now nothing exercises this new function at all.

findings.title: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction block
findings.body: Postgres rejects `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` inside a transaction block (`ERROR: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block`). This file also contains a `CREATE TABLE` (lines 1-6), so if the migration runner wraps each file in a transaction — the common default — the whole migration aborts at deploy time. It also fails partway differently on retry: a cancelled CONCURRENTLY build leaves an INVALID index behind that must be dropped manually before re-running. If the runner does not disable transactions per-file, this statement needs to move to its own non-transactional migration. Note that if the duplicate-index issue above is addressed by removing the statement, this concern goes away with it.

findings.title: priority=9 delays reset email; scale is inverted (0 drains first)
findings.body:
`enqueue`'s docstring states the priority argument is an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last**, and explicitly warns that the name suggests the opposite. Passing `priority=9` therefore puts password-reset mail behind every other job on the queue, including the nightly digest batch this PR was trying to jump ahead of. It is also strictly worse than the previous behaviour, which used the default of 5.

To achieve the stated intent, pass `priority=0` (or a low value such as 1 if some class of job must still precede it).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 delays reset mail to last in queue, inverting intent

findings.title: No test asserts reset email is enqueued ahead of other jobs
findings.body: The change sets priority=9 to move reset emails 'ahead' of the digest batch, but per queue/priority.py's docstring, priority runs 0 (drained first) to 9 (drained last) — the opposite of what the name suggests. There is no test in this diff (or apparent in the repo) that asserts send_reset_email's job is actually drained before a lower-priority job, so if the intended fix is backwards (as the docstring suggests it may be), nothing would catch it.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised title terms
findings.body: `upsert` documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and explicitly states it does not normalise: a term differing only by case creates a separate posting list that lower-casing queries will never match, and the document is then silently unfindable by that term. `article.title.split()` yields the raw words, which for essentially every real title include capitalised words (titles are usually title-cased). Pass normalised terms instead, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {w.lower() for w in article.title.split()})`, or move normalisation into `upsert` itself.

findings.title: New publish→index behavior has no test, and would not catch the unnormalised-terms bug
findings.body: publish() now calls upsert(article.id, article.title.split()), passing raw, non-lower-cased, non-deduplicated terms straight from the title. Per search/index.py's own docstring, upsert does not normalise terms — case-differing terms create separate posting lists that queries (which do lower-case) will never match, so an article silently becomes unfindable by any word in its title that isn't already lowercase. No test exists for publish() indexing behavior, so nothing exercises upsert with a realistic title (e.g. containing a capitalized word) and asserts the article is actually retrievable by search. A test that published an article with a mixed-case title and then queried for a lower-cased term would have caught this.

findings.title: Referer header logged unscrubbed, leaking auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch specifically special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before storing it. The replacement copies `request.headers[header]` verbatim for all four headers, so the `Referer` value is now written straight into the log via `log_method(json.dumps(headers, ...))` on line 6.

Per the retrieved `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and the docstring there explicitly notes the browser sends that token back in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. Any 5xx therefore writes a live auth token to the server log, where it is readable by anyone with log access (and any log shipping/aggregation downstream).

Restore the scrubbing for `Referer` (and keep threading `extra_param_keys` into it) rather than logging the raw value. If the goal is to see what the client sent, the scrubbed URI already preserves everything except the sensitive query parameters.

Also note that dropping the only use of `extra_param_keys` here likely leaves that parameter unused in this function, which is a signal the removal was unintentional rather than a deliberate policy change.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked into server logs via unscrubbed Referer header

findings.body: The change deletes the call to `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` that previously sanitized the Referer header before logging (per identity.py, Referer carries the auth token via token_authenticated_url). findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets project query param traverse paths in file DAO
findings.body:
`list` reads the caller-supplied `project` query parameter via `query.GetProjectQueryParam()` and, after this change, passes it downstream with no identifier validation at all. The file-backed DAO builds its on-disk path with `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and its doc comment states plainly: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." `filepath.Join` normalises `..` segments rather than rejecting them, so `?project=../../etc` resolves outside `d.Folder` and the join provides no confinement.

Adversary: any client that can reach the list endpoint. What they control: the full `project` query string. What they get: reads of documents outside the configured storage root, and — since the same project name is the unit of authorisation elsewhere — a way to address resources under a project they were not scoped to.

The remaining check on lines 4-6 only compares the query value against a path parameter when one is present; it is a consistency check, not a character-set validation, and it does nothing when the request has no path project. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` call, or push equivalent validation into `buildPath` before relying on the join.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Removing ValidateID breaks buildPath's documented caller contract

findings.title: No test guards removal of project-name validation on the list path
findings.body: The removed call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) was the only check that the query-parameter project name is a safe identifier before it flows into path construction (buildPath joins it verbatim per file.go). Since no test file is included in this diff, there is nothing that would fail if this removal reintroduces path traversal or otherwise invalid names reaching downstream storage code. A test asserting that a malicious/invalid projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing '../' or other invalid characters) is now accepted instead of rejected — or conversely, one that fails to catch its being silently accepted — is needed here.

findings.title: Buffer reserved from client-declared Content-Length (memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory based on a length the client declares, before any of the body has actually been read. In the S3 UploadPart path this value originates from the request's `Content-Length` header (or the equivalent part-size field), so an attacker who can reach the `serve s3` endpoint can send `Content-Length: 5368709120` with a one-byte body and make the process reserve gigabytes; a handful of concurrent requests OOM-kill the server. Previously the buffer grew a page at a time as bytes actually arrived, so cost was bounded by bytes delivered — that natural bound is what this change removes.

Mitigations: clamp the reservation to a modest cap (`min(contentLength, maxReserve)`) so the reservation is a hint rather than a promise, and/or wrap `body` in an `io.LimitReader(body, contentLength)` plus reject parts above the configured maximum part size before allocating. Growth beyond the clamp then remains driven by bytes genuinely received.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Negative contentLength (unknown/chunked body) passed to Reserve unchecked

findings.title: No test exercises Reserve(contentLength) with mismatched/large lengths
findings.body: The change pre-allocates the multipart buffer based on the caller-supplied contentLength. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) verifying behavior when contentLength is 0, negative, larger than the actual body, or attacker-controlled to be very large (the scenario this PR is presumably fixing/mitigating). Without such a test, a regression that reintroduces unbounded allocation, or a bug in Reserve's handling of bad lengths, would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Default flipped from HTTPS to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The original expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selects plaintext when the caller explicitly sets `is_secure=False`; every other case — including the overwhelmingly common one where `is_secure` is absent and `.get()` returns `None` — yields `https`. The replacement `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` as falsy, so any request that does not explicitly opt in to TLS is now sent over `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com...`, transmitting the request (and any AWS auth headers built for it) in the clear.

If the ternary must be written in positive form, preserve the default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`. Note the second form still differs from the original for non-boolean falsy values (`0`, `""`), so the `is False` comparison is the faithful preservation of the prior contract.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset

findings.title: No test covers the changed default scheme behavior
findings.body: The scheme selection logic changed: previously the default (when is_secure is absent, None, or truthy-but-not-False) resolved to "https"; now the default (when is_secure is absent, None, or falsy) resolves to "http". This flips the default security posture for requests that don't explicitly set is_secure. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing exercises download_request with is_secure unset/None/True/False to confirm the resulting scheme is correct. If this change is wrong, a request with no is_secure key would silently be downgraded to plaintext HTTP and no test would fail.

findings.title: DELETE now maps to "push", granting deletes to push-only accounts
findings.body:
The previous switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `"delete"` action; the new two-branch form only ever produces `"pull"` or `"push"`, so a DELETE request is authorized against the `push` permission. Any account granted push (e.g. CI publishing tags) can now delete existing tags/manifests/blobs, and any policy that deliberately withholds `delete` is silently ineffective. The `"delete"` action becomes unreachable, so the access-control config for it is dead. Restore the `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (or an equivalent `if m == http.MethodDelete` before the push fallback).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE requests now authorised as "push", bypassing delete permission

findings.title: Comment on distinct push/delete actions no longer matches behavior
findings.body: config.go documents that ActionPush and ActionDelete are "distinct on purpose" so an account can be allowed to push without being allowed to delete. This diff maps HTTP DELETE to the "push" action instead of a separate "delete" action, so that documented invariant is no longer true: any account with push access now also has delete access. Either update the config.go comment to reflect the new policy, or restore the distinct delete mapping.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE now mapping to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The mapping change causes HTTP DELETE requests to be authorized under the 'push' action instead of the previously distinct 'delete' action. The repository's own config comments state these actions are 'distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones' — this change collapses that distinction. No test in this diff (or referenced) asserts that DELETE maps to a specific action, so this authorization behavior change would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: Unknown methods (e.g. OPTIONS) default to "push" instead of "pull"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm assigned `"pull"` for any method not explicitly listed — notably OPTIONS, and anything else reaching this handler. The new negated condition treats every method other than GET/HEAD as push, so previously-permitted requests (CORS preflight OPTIONS, for example) will now be evaluated against push permissions and can be rejected for read-only clients. If the intent is to keep the permissive default, gate the push branch on the explicit write-method set rather than on "not a read method".

findings.title: Overflow handling clears the entry just written and the whole cache
findings.body: `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` is immediately followed by `if len(_CACHE) > 1000: _CACHE.clear()`. When the threshold is crossed, the entry this function just populated is thrown away along with every other cached tenant, so the stated purpose ("a live fetch into the shared cache") silently fails for that call and a subsequent `get_tenant(tenant_id)` returns `None`. Every other caller also takes a full cold-cache hit at an arbitrary moment. Use a bounded eviction policy instead (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)` or `functools.lru_cache`-style bounding), or at minimum evict before inserting and never evict the key just fetched.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh's fetch/cache/eviction logic
findings.body: The new function fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared cache, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so a regression (e.g. caching before fetch succeeds, an off-by-one in the eviction threshold, or clearing on the wrong condition) would go undetected.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh's full-cache-clear side effect isn't documented
findings.body: The name and signature suggest a simple fresh-fetch-and-cache helper, but the function also unconditionally clears the entire shared cache (all tenants, not just this one) once it exceeds 1000 entries. A caller relying on the name alone would not expect calling this for one tenant could evict every other cached tenant. A short docstring or comment noting the eviction behavior would prevent misuse.

findings.title: Renaming --workers changes args.workers to args.concurrency
findings.body: `argparse` derives the destination attribute from the option name, so after this change the parsed namespace exposes `args.concurrency` and no longer exposes `args.workers`. Any code that reads `args.workers` will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime, and any existing shell script or CI invocation passing `--workers 8` will fail with "unrecognized arguments". No consumer of `parser()` was updated in this diff. If the intent is only to align the user-facing name with the internal one, prefer `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)` so the old spelling keeps working, and update every reader of `args.workers`.

findings.title: README still documents removed `--workers` flag
findings.body:
cli.py renames `--workers` to `--concurrency`, but README.md line 7 still says "`--workers` — how many worker processes to start." A user following the README would pass a flag that no longer exists. Update this line to `--concurrency`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Flag rename has no visible test coverage
findings.body: The --workers flag was renamed to --concurrency, a breaking change for any script or user invoking the old flag name. No test file is included in this diff to verify that parser() now accepts --concurrency (and no longer accepts --workers, if that matters). If any existing test asserted on '--workers' by name, it would need updating; if none exists, this rename ships without any check that argument parsing still works correctly.

findings.title: Docstring says integer total; code now returns dict
findings.body: The docstring 'Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer.' is no longer true. The function now returns a dict mapping day -> count (line 4). A caller relying on the docstring would treat the return value as an int and break. Update the docstring to describe the new per-day dict return shape.
